records.sourceFile: Using bar velocity to assess post-match neuromuscular fatigue in young soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Barreira J, Gantois P, Castro J, Mesquita X, Peixoto R, Cid MF, et al. Using Bar Velocity to Assess Post-match Neuromuscular Fatigue in Young Soccer Players. Int J Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: The study tracked jump and bar-velocity measures in 21 U-19 soccer players before and after official matches. Countermovement jump stayed impaired to 24 h, half-squat velocity recovered by 24 h, hip-thrust velocity stayed reduced to 48 h, and bench press and horizontal jump showed no sustained decline.
paper.tldr: Hip-thrust bar velocity stayed reduced for about two days after a youth match, while half-squat velocity recovered by 24 h and bench press was not affected. Use this to shape which loaded exercises are programmed on the first days after a match, not as a fixed recovery timeline.
paper.methods: This cross-sectional repeated-measures study tested 21 U-19 players before, 30 minutes after, 24 h after and 48 h after official matches. Loads were set at about 70% of an estimated 1RM from a submaximal load-velocity profile, velocity was recorded with a linear encoder, and jumps were measured with a contact mat and a standard horizontal jump. Analysis used generalised estimating equations with Holm-Bonferroni post-hoc tests.
paper.findings: Countermovement jump fell 6.79% immediately after the match (p = 0.036), stayed reduced at 24 h (p = 0.050, effect size -0.82), and was not different at 48 h. Half-squat velocity fell 6.8% after the match (p = 0.004) and was back to baseline at 24 h and 48 h. Hip-thrust velocity fell 12.3% after the match and remained reduced at 24 h (p < 0.001) and 48 h (p < 0.001). Bench press showed no change at any time point, and horizontal jump increased at 48 h (p < 0.001). Many 24 h values had large missing data.
paper.limitations: The authors used a cross-sectional design with a small sample, submaximal estimated loads and non-randomised exercise order. Some percentages differ between the abstract and results, and reported percentages do not always match the reported means (the half-squat drop is given as 6.8% and 5.05%, while 0.67 to 0.64 m/s is about 4.5%); the horizontal jump row for 24 h also repeats the 48 h value. Missing data at 24 h were 41 to 45% for several measures, and training load and wellbeing were not monitored.
paper.practicalImplications: Consider avoiding hip-thrust and other posterior-chain loading at MD+1 and MD+2, and use half-squat and bench press in the first days after a match if the aim is to keep strength work in the week. Track bar velocity at fixed loads as a quick readiness check, but confirm changes against the athlete's own baseline.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Use bar-velocity tracking during routine lifts to check readiness at MD+1 and MD+2 without an extra test. Treat heavy hip-thrust and other glute and hamstring loading with caution on MD+1 and MD+2, because hip-thrust velocity was still reduced at 48 h while half-squat velocity had recovered by 24 h.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: The study measured healthy players after matches and did not include injured athletes or return-to-play criteria. It cannot be used to decide when an injured player can return to play.
